title: No place for the tiger
hookLine: one who knows how to live meets no tiger, for there's no place in him for its claws (Tao Te Ching 50)

cards: A traveler is crossing wild country. There are rhinoceroses in the long grass, tigers in the hills, and somewhere up ahead, soldiers. A sensible traveler would plan a route around all of it.
Chapter fifty of the Tao Te Ching describes someone who walks straight through and comes out untouched. The odd part is the explanation. The chapter never says the tiger is gone, or tame, or asleep.
It says the tiger can't find anywhere on this person to hold on.

teach.h: CLUTCHING AT LIFE IS ITS OWN DANGER.
teach.b: First, where the chapter starts. Not with tigers, but with life and death. People come out into life and go back into death, it says, and some hurry toward death by straining too hard to keep living.

Clutching at life, in this chapter, is its own danger. Second, the traveler. In James Legge's translation, the one who manages his life well walks the land without having to dodge the rhinoceros or the tiger.

teach.h: THE TIGER FINDS NO PLACE FOR ITS CLAWS.
teach.b: The rhinoceros finds no place for its horn, "nor the tiger a place in which to fix its claws," nor the weapon a place for its point. Why? "Because there is in him no place of death."
Third, what that might mean. Some readers take it close to the letter, as a picture of a charmed life. Others hear it as a map of the inside.
Claws need a handhold. Insult needs pride to wound. Fear needs something gripped too tightly.
Greed needs a hunger to hook. Where there's less clutching, there's less to catch. Fourth, closer in.
A sharp email lands. A comment stings in a meeting. Notice where it bites.
It may be the spot that was already sore, the reputation you're guarding, the point you need to win. The chapter makes no promise that hard things won't come.
It points at the handhold, the place the claws were going to grab, and suggests there could be less of it.

how: Readers of the Tao Te Ching take chapter fifty in more than one way: some as a picture of the sage's protected life, others as a teaching that less clutching leaves less for harm to grip.

games.q: what does “no place for the tiger” mean?
o: a land where all the wild tigers are gone
a charm said to keep wild animals far away
having nothing the tiger's claws can grab onto

p: finds no place for its horn

s: chapter fifty says the tiger has been tamed
it says nothing of taming; the tiger simply finds no place in the traveler to fix its claws.
the chapter says some hurry toward death by straining to live
it opens with life and death, and with people who clutch at life too hard.
the chapter promises nothing hard will ever happen
it pictures a traveler with no handhold for harm; some readers take it literally, others as a teaching about the inside.

games.q: you're the traveler in chapter fifty. tigers in the hills, soldiers ahead. what does the chapter say the skilled one does?
o: walks on; the tiger finds nowhere to grip.
games.why: the skilled traveler walks the land without having to dodge the tiger, because there is in him no place of death.

practice: Bring to mind one small danger on your horizon, like a hard conversation, a bill or a result you're waiting for, and notice where it grips: the jaw, the stomach, a story about what it will say about you.
On an out-breath, let that spot loosen a little. If the worry comes back, meet it the same way, calmly, again.

wordCard.voice: No place for the tiger. Chapter fifty's traveler: the tiger finds nowhere to fix its claws, because there is no place of death in him. Today's word.

orig.note: Chinese: tiger. chapter fifty pairs it with the rhinoceros.

carryVoice: Your line: no place for claws. Hard things may still come; the grip is what can loosen. I'll be here tomorrow.
